units.title: Unit 19 — Social life
learningObjectives: Use natural collocations for casual visits, parties, celebrations and time spent with friends.
Distinguish informal social expressions from the formal language of official invitations and hosting.
Apply accurate verb and noun pairings for events, hospitality, dining and special occasions.
Explain nuances such as a flying visit versus a whirlwind visit and playing host to versus playing the host.

items.example: Our cousins made a flying visit before catching their train north.
items.note: A flying visit is short, usually with little time to settle in or catch up.

items.example: They planned a girls' night out after months of conflicting schedules.
items.note: A girls' night out is an informal evening spent socialising with female friends.

items.example: We often go out for a meal after our monthly book-club meeting.
items.note: Go out for a meal describes eating at a restaurant rather than at home.

items.example: It can be difficult to stick to a diet during a long holiday.
items.note: Stick to means continue following a plan despite temptation or difficulty.

items.example: The team arranged a surprise party for their retiring supervisor.
items.note: A surprise party is organised without the guest of honour knowing in advance.

items.example: The children hoped to spring a surprise on their grandmother at lunch.
items.note: Spring a surprise on someone stresses that the news or event is unexpected.

items.example: Reaching the funding goal would certainly call for a celebration.
items.note: Call for means justify or make an event or response appropriate.

items.example: They decided to throw a party to welcome their new neighbours.
items.note: Throw a party is a common informal alternative to organise or host a party.

items.pt: aparecer por pouco tempo em um evento
items.example: Even the busy director managed to put in an appearance at the farewell dinner.
items.note: Put in an appearance often implies attending briefly or despite other commitments.

items.example: The family saved the homemade dessert for a special occasion.
items.note: Special occasion refers to a meaningful event that merits recognition.

items.example: We try to spend quality time together without checking our phones.
items.note: Quality time emphasises focused, meaningful attention rather than duration alone.

items.pt: visita rápida e cheia de atividades
items.example: They managed a whirlwind visit that included three museums and a family reunion.
items.note: A whirlwind visit is both brief and very busy; it is not merely a short stay.

items.example: After moving to the city, she found herself caught up in a social whirl.
items.note: A social whirl is a rapid succession of social engagements and activities.

items.pt: sair para dançar em casas noturnas
items.example: Some colleagues still go clubbing together on Friday nights.
items.note: Go clubbing is informal for visiting nightclubs, often to dance.

items.example: An old school friend contacted me after twenty years abroad.
items.note: School friend identifies someone known from school, not necessarily an elderly person.

items.pt: convidar alguém para acompanhar um programa
items.example: You can invite someone along if they would enjoy the picnic.
items.note: Invite someone along means ask the person to accompany a group or join an outing.

items.example: The library will play host to a festival of experimental poetry this autumn.
items.note: Play host to is relatively formal and can refer to hosting people or major events.

items.example: The organisers held a welcome reception for visiting researchers.
items.note: A welcome reception is an organised social event held to greet arrivals.

items.example: Small gestures can make someone feel welcome on their first day.
items.note: Make someone feel welcome stresses the visitor’s experience; make someone welcome can also occur.

items.example: Our manager promised to find time to meet the volunteers.
items.note: Find time to do something means make room for it in a busy schedule.

items.example: The mayor will pay a visit to the new cultural centre next week.
items.note: Pay a visit is somewhat formal; pay is followed by a visit, often with to.

items.example: Local residents were invited to join the festivities in the central square.
items.note: Festivities are organised celebrations; join the festivities is common in invitations.

items.example: All scholarship recipients will attend a formal function in December.
items.note: Formal function refers to an organised ceremonial or official social event.

items.word: mark the closing of the festival
items.example: A short concert will mark the closing of the festival on Sunday evening.
items.note: Mark the closing of identifies the event or act commemorating an ending.

items.example: A family gathering can be a relaxed alternative to a large celebration.
items.note: A gathering is a meeting of people, usually less formal than an official function.

items.pt: receber alguém com jantar e bebidas de forma requintada
items.example: The hosts planned to wine and dine their overseas guests after the conference.
items.note: Wine and dine someone means entertain the person generously with food and drink.

items.example: Soft music and shared tables created a convivial atmosphere.
items.note: Convivial is a rather formal adjective meaning sociable, friendly and welcoming.

items.pt: o local ideal para um evento
items.example: The restored theatre is the perfect venue for the awards ceremony.
items.note: Venue names a place used for an organised event, not simply any location.

items.example: The neighbours offered to organise a barbecue for the whole street.
items.note: Use organise or have with barbecue, not make a barbecue; organise is British spelling.

items.example: We might have a barbecue if the weather improves on Saturday.
items.note: Have a barbecue describes holding the event, while organise stresses arranging it.

items.example: The staff are collecting photographs for a retirement party in June.
items.note: Retirement party is a conventional name for a celebration of someone's retirement.

items.example: They hope to give a dinner party for their closest friends next month.
items.note: Give a dinner party means host a planned meal at home or another venue.

items.example: Families may eat out more often during school holidays.
items.note: Eat out describes eating at a restaurant instead of preparing food at home.

items.pt: pedir comida para viagem ou entrega
items.example: We decided to order a takeaway rather than cook after the journey.
items.note: Takeaway is chiefly British for prepared food collected or delivered for eating elsewhere.

items.example: The hotel offered plain food for guests who disliked rich sauces.
items.note: Plain food is simple and usually not heavily seasoned or elaborate.

items.example: Some people avoid rich food late at night because it feels heavy.
items.note: Rich food is heavy or substantial, often containing plenty of fat or cream.

items.example: At the annual dinner, the department head likes to play the host.
items.note: Play the host focuses on acting as a host, whereas play host to names guests or events.

units.title: Unit 20 — Talking
learningObjectives: Use established expressions to initiate, maintain and end conversations appropriately.
Distinguish neutral exchanges from emotionally personal conversations, rumours and arguments.
Select natural collocations for introducing difficult topics and responding to disagreement.
Differentiate levels of offensiveness, types of promises and conversation-opening language.

items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: The passengers passed the time with idle chatter about the weather.
items.note: Idle chatter is casual talk with no serious purpose; it is not necessarily negative.

items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: The two speakers stopped to exchange pleasantries before the panel began.
items.note: Exchange pleasantries is relatively formal for brief, polite social conversation.

items.pt: fofoca picante ou cheia de detalhes
items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: The magazine promises juicy gossip about famous performers.
items.note: Juicy suggests intriguing, personal or potentially scandalous details and is informal.

items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: We meet once a month to exchange news about our former classmates.
items.note: Exchange news means each participant shares updates, not necessarily gossip.

items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: Anonymous accounts can spread rumours before anyone checks the facts.
items.note: Spread rumours means circulate unverified claims, often with harmful consequences.

items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: After major announcements, rumours fly around the office for several days.
items.note: The idiomatic image of rumours flying around suggests uncontrolled circulation.

items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: A volunteer tried to engage someone in conversation while they waited.
items.note: Engage someone in conversation means draw a person into talking, usually politely.

items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: It takes trust to open your heart to someone about a painful experience.
items.note: Open your heart to someone means share private feelings honestly and openly.

items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: I would rather leave than get drawn into an argument online.
items.note: Get drawn into describes becoming involved in a dispute, sometimes reluctantly.

items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: You do not always need to win an argument to reach an agreement.
items.note: Win an argument means persuade others or prevail in a dispute, not win a physical contest.

items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: It is possible to lose an argument but still learn something useful.
items.note: Lose an argument means fail to prevail in a disagreement; it is not lose your temper.

items.pt: gostar de uma boa discussão de ideias
items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: Our reading group members enjoy a good discussion about difficult topics.
items.note: A good discussion focuses on exchanging ideas and need not become an argument.

items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: The music was so loud that we could barely carry on a conversation.
items.note: Carry on a conversation means continue talking rather than carry out a task.

items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: The room was quiet enough to hold a conversation without shouting.
items.note: Hold a conversation means conduct an exchange with another person.

items.pt: manter uma conversa educada e superficial
items.section: A · Types of language and conversation
items.example: They tried to make polite conversation while waiting for the interview.
items.note: Make polite conversation refers to socially appropriate small talk.

items.example: She struggled to broach the subject of unpaid expenses at the meeting.
items.note: Broach the subject often implies introducing an uncomfortable or sensitive topic.

items.example: When the debate became personal, the moderator chose to change the subject.
items.note: Change the subject means shift to a different topic; the motive may vary.

items.pt: levantar ou trazer um assunto à conversa
items.example: We can bring up the subject of flexible hours after the main agenda.
items.note: Bring up the subject is a neutral, common alternative to broach the subject.

items.example: It is important to take someone seriously when they report a safety concern.
items.note: Take someone seriously means treat their views or concerns as worthy of attention.

items.pt: exagerar a força dos próprios argumentos
items.example: You may weaken your proposal if you overstate your case in the introduction.
items.note: Overstate your case means exaggerate the importance or strength of your position.

items.example: It is unfair to bombard someone with questions before they have prepared.
items.note: Bombard someone with questions is an emphatic metaphor for asking many questions rapidly.

items.example: It is unhelpful to make broad generalisations about an entire generation.
items.note: Broad generalisations are sweeping claims that overlook important differences.

items.example: We agreed to drop the subject until everyone had read the report.
items.note: Drop the subject means stop discussing it, not introduce it again.

items.example: The broadcaster warned viewers that the film contained bad language.
items.note: Bad language is a general expression for swearing or offensive words.

items.example: The notice warned parents about strong language in the performance.
items.note: Strong language often means swearing but can also imply forceful wording.

items.example: The referee cautioned the player for using foul language.
items.note: Foul language is particularly offensive and stronger than bad language.

items.example: The interview was edited to remove several four-letter words.
items.note: Four-letter words is an informal euphemism for swear words, not simply any short words.

items.pt: abordagem inicial para começar uma conversa
items.example: His light-hearted remark was an opening gambit that helped people relax at the event.
items.note: An opening gambit is the first move or remark intended to start an exchange.

items.example: Agreeing to finish overnight would be a rash promise without checking the workload.
items.note: A rash promise is made too quickly or without considering the consequences.

items.pt: promessa vazia que não será cumprida
items.example: Offering help without any intention to act is an empty promise.
items.note: An empty promise is not sincerely intended or is unlikely to be fulfilled.

items.example: Whether the policy is fair is a tough question with no easy answer.
items.note: Tough means difficult to answer or confront, not physically hard.

items.example: Some managers make empty promises about promotions they cannot offer.
items.note: Make empty promises highlights the action of promising without genuine commitment.

items.example: The review committee is expected to ask tough questions about the budget.
items.note: Ask tough questions is natural when interviewers seek difficult, revealing answers.

items.example: Posting a provocation online can draw someone into an argument.
items.note: Draw someone into contrasts the active cause with get drawn into, which centres the participant.
